text: Chapter 26, the payment system. In a few minutes, let's see how one payment is never charged twice, and never missed.

First, the pay-in flow. The user places an order. The payment service stores the event, then hands it to the payment executor. The executor saves the order in its own database, and calls an external payment service provider, or PSP, to charge the card. Once the charge succeeds, we update the wallet, and finally record an entry in the ledger.

A payment order has four states: not started, executing, success, and failed. Notice that executing in our database does not mean the PSP has charged anything. The wallet and the ledger each have their own flag, so every step can be tracked on its own.

The ledger uses double-entry bookkeeping. Every movement of money is recorded in two accounts. The buyer pays one dollar, the seller receives one dollar. In each transaction, total debits equal total credits. So money can be traced end to end, and reconciliation has something to check against.

The hard part is the timeout. The executor calls the PSP, and no response comes back. All you know is that nothing arrived. Maybe the request never got there. Or maybe the money was already charged, and only the response was lost on the way.

Now suppose we retry with a brand new request ID. What happens? The PSP sees a new payment, and charges again. The buyer pays twice. A retry must happen at least once, but it must never become a double charge.

The fix is idempotency. On retry, reuse the original payment order ID as the idempotency key. The PSP sees a key it has already processed, so it does not charge again, and returns the earlier result. Our own database does the same, with a unique constraint that rejects a duplicate insert.

Retries also need a rhythm. We use exponential backoff: each wait is twice as long as the one before. Failures that can be retried go to a retry queue. If a payment still fails after the retry limit, it moves to a dead letter queue, for people to investigate.

Even then, systems can still disagree. So every night, the PSP sends a settlement file. We compare it with our internal records, one payment at a time, and look for differences. Known kinds are fixed by a standard procedure. The rest go to the finance team, to handle by hand.

Remember three words: idempotency key, reconciliation, double-entry bookkeeping. Record first, then call out. When unsure, check. Retry with the same key. And let reconciliation catch whatever is left.
